hook: A leadership expert spent years pouring encouragement into his struggling son and watched him shrink. The problem was never the boy. It was the way his father was seeing him.

sections.h: The Problem Is How You See
p: Stephen Covey and his wife tried everything with their son: cheering, coaching, modelling a positive attitude. Nothing worked. Then Covey noticed something uncomfortable in himself. Underneath all the encouragement, he did not actually believe the boy was okay. He saw him as someone who needed fixing, and the boy was receiving that message rather than the words. So they stopped trying to change the boy and changed their own seeing instead. Given room, he flourished.

Covey calls the mental map you carry a paradigm. We do not see the world as it is, he says, we see it as we are. And when your map is wrong, working harder on top of it just gets you more efficiently lost. He proved this to classrooms with a famous drawing that reads as either a young woman or an old crone depending on which image you were shown for ten seconds beforehand. Ten seconds of conditioning made students certain, and made them dismiss anyone who disagreed. You have been conditioned for decades.
sections.pull: The way you see the problem is the problem.

p: For his doctoral work Covey read two centuries of American success writing and watched a shift happen. The early material was about character: integrity, humility, courage, patience, the Golden Rule. The later material was about personality: image, attitude, influence tricks, how to get people to like you. Quicker, easier, and built on sand.

You cannot fake a marriage with communication techniques. What you are shouts so loudly that people cannot hear what you say. Covey gives two images for why. First, the law of the farm: you can cram for an exam, but you cannot cram a harvest. Skip planting in spring and no amount of autumn panic produces a crop. Second, a battleship signalling an approaching light to change course, escalating from captain to battleship, until the reply comes back: I am a lighthouse. Principles do not move for your rank or your urgency.

sections.h: Be Proactive, Begin With The End
p: Habit one rests on Viktor Frankl's discovery in the death camps: between what happens to you and how you respond lies a gap, and in that gap is your freedom. Listen to your language, Covey says. He makes me so mad and I have to are the vocabulary of a victim. I choose and I will keep the power with you. Draw two circles: everything you care about, and inside it the smaller set of things you can actually affect. Reactive people pour energy into the outer ring and watch their influence shrink. Proactive people work the inner ring and watch it grow.

Habit two asks you to picture your own funeral and decide what you want four speakers to say. Those answers are your real values. All things are created twice, mentally then physically, and if you skip the first creation someone else's script fills the gap. Covey separates leadership from management with a jungle: workers hacking through undergrowth, managers sharpening machetes and writing schedules, and a leader who climbs the tallest tree and shouts wrong jungle. Management is climbing the ladder efficiently. Leadership decides which wall it leans against.
sections.pull: We climb the ladder of success only to find, at the top, that it was leaning against the wrong wall.

p: Picture a square divided in four. Across the top, urgent and not urgent. Down the side, important and not important. Quadrant one is crises. Quadrant three is interruptions and other people's urgency. Quadrant four is time wasted. Quadrant two is the important but not urgent: planning, exercise, relationships, learning, prevention. Most people bounce between one and three all day and collapse into four for relief.

Effective people live in quadrant two, and the more they do, the smaller quadrant one becomes, because the fires get prevented. But nothing external will ever push you toward quadrant two. You have to schedule it first, before the week fills, which means saying no to plenty of urgent things. You can only say no peacefully when you have a bigger yes burning inside.

Covey organises weekly rather than daily, around roles rather than tasks. List your roles, pick one or two important goals for each, and block those first. Do not schedule your priorities, prioritise your schedule.

The most beloved passage in the book is about a lawn. Covey delegated the yard to his seven year old son, but spent two weeks training first. Green and clean, that was the job. He walked the neighbourhood pointing at yards. He asked who the boss would be. You are, said the boy. No, said Covey. You boss yourself. I am your helper. They agreed to walk the yard together twice a week.

Then the hard part. For two weeks nothing happened. The grass yellowed, the rubbish piled up, and Covey watched through the window, dying inside. On the walk-around the boy's lip quivered and he burst into tears. It's so hard, Dad. The temptation to snap or to rescue was enormous. Covey said only, is there anything I can do to help, because he had promised to be the helper. From that moment the boy owned the yard, and kept it better than his father had.

This is stewardship delegation rather than gofer delegation: agree the desired result, the guidelines, the resources, the accountability and the consequences, then leave the method alone. The moment you take the job back to relieve your own discomfort, you have taught the person they were never really responsible.
sections.pull: The instant you rescue someone from a job you gave them, you take the job back for good.

p: Covey calls habit five the key to all the others. Most of us do not listen to understand, we listen to reply. He compares it to an optician who hears you complain for thirty seconds, hands you his own glasses and says just try harder, they work great for me. We prescribe before we diagnose constantly, and call it helping.

His demonstration is a teenager who says, Dad, school is for the birds. Every instinct says lecture. Instead the father just reflects the feeling back, exchange after exchange, until several layers down the boy finally says the real thing: I'm scared. I don't think I can read well enough for college. That was the problem all along, and one sentence of advice at the start would have buried it permanently.

Then comes win-win, which Covey insists is a system and not an attitude. He describes a chief executive complaining that his people would not cooperate, then showing Covey a wall chart of salesmen racing each other to a trip to Bermuda. Companies reward A while hoping for B. And he defines maturity beautifully: the balance of courage and consideration. Courage without consideration is win-lose. Consideration without courage is lose-win. Both at full strength is the only thing that works.

sections.h: Sharpen The Saw, Then Break The Chain
p: A man saws furiously at a tree, exhausted. Take a break and sharpen the saw, you suggest. I don't have time, he says, I'm too busy sawing. Habit seven is renewal in four dimensions: physical, mental, social and emotional, and spiritual. Neglect one and the others suffer. Covey ties it to the goose that laid golden eggs. Kill the goose for a quick harvest and you get nothing, forever. The eggs are your results. The goose is you.

The idea he saves for last is the one that stays with people. Every one of us inherits scripts, and some of that inheritance is damage, handed down by people who were handed it themselves and never noticed they were passing anything on. A transition person is someone who stops the transmission. Nobody gives you a medal for the cruelty you absorbed and did not repeat. Covey thought it was among the most powerful things a human being can do with a life.
sections.pull: Being proactive means you are not obligated to repeat what was done to you.

takeaways: Catch your reactive language this week and replace it deliberately: swap I have to and he makes me feel for I choose and I will.
Spend an hour drafting a personal mission statement, starting from the question of what you want said about you at your funeral.
Run the thirty day test: for one month work only inside your circle of influence, make small commitments and keep them, and never argue about anyone else's weaknesses.
Organise weekly rather than daily. List your roles, pick one important goal for each, and schedule those blocks before the week fills up.
Delegate one thing properly: agree the result, the guidelines, the resources and the check-in, then keep your hands off the method even when it goes badly.
In your next tense conversation, reflect the other person's feeling back until they confirm you have it, before you say a single word of your own view.
Book renewal time in all four dimensions this week: one workout, one hour of reading, one real conversation, and one period of quiet reflection.
